newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy stock revival ups chances for privatisations.
newsitem.headline: Italy stock revival ups chances for privatisations.

text.p: A revival in the fortunes of Milan's stock exchange, which burst into life last week after months in the doldrums, offers the government a unique chance to speed up a sell-off of state assets, Italian commentators said.

The bourse's Mib30 index, which measures the performance of the top 30 listed companies in the country, closed 9.04 percent higher on Friday from a week earlier, driven by a wave of buying mainly by domestic investors.
Turnover in stocks on Friday was the second highest in the history of the market at 2.2 trillion lire ($1.46 billion).

Italian weekend newspapers were full of articles quoting market pundits proffering advice on whether the bourse, which last year lagged behind other European stock exchanges, had finally turned the corner.

Commentators were agreed on thing -- Italian investors are looking for a profitable alternative to salting their money away in government bonds as falling interest rates eat away at a once-secure source of income.

Domestic savers -- nicknamed "Bot people" after the most widely bought treasury instrument -- have clung for a generation to the secure life-raft provided by government bonds issued on attractive terms to fund Italy's huge public sector deficit.

The government, which has said it wants to privatise two giant state concerns this year -- telecoms group Stet and electrical utility Enel -- now has a golden opportunity to cash in on the public's hunger for new investments.
"The bourse is in an ideal condition to be able to welcome even massive flotations," said Ferruccio De Bortoli in Milan dialy newspaper Corriere della Sera.

"The opportunity is great, unrepeatable. And a new disappointment would be devastating -- it would compromise the slow, even if contradictory, process of growth of our financial market," De Bortoli said.
The Milan stock exchange, with only 215 companies listed, has traditionally been looked upon with suspicion by most Italians as an exclusive club where outsiders fear to tread.
But with yields on short-term treasury bills barely more than five percent, the temptation for small investors to try their luck on the stock exchange is proving hard to resist.

The Italian fund management association reported last week that investors were putting more of their savings in equity mutual funds (unit trusts). Net subscriptions rose in December for the first time for two years.

The successful sale by the government over the past year of two tranches of shares in energy group ENI, which were eagerly snapped up by Italian households, has shown the appetite for privatisation stocks is strong.
But Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government may fail to strike while the iron is hot, analysts said.
Disagreements within the government over how to go about merging Stet with its subsidiary Telecom Italia in preparation for a sell-off suggest there could be delays in privatising the merged entity.
The government also has to assemble a "hard core" of shareholders in Stet, to ensure that the group remains under Italian control.
